Publication date: 1 January 2027

Source: Brain Research, Volume 1894

Author(s): Yating Bai, Qingfang Zhang

articles.title: Neurotransmitter receptor architecture links local neurochemistry to semantic memory
articles.content: A fundamental challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the molecular and neurochemical architecture of the human cortex gives rise to sophisticated higher cognitive functions. The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is a key hub for semantic memory, and its underlying GABAergic and glutamatergic neurochemistry supports semantic memory performance. However, the molecular receptor architecture underlying these neurochemical-cognitive relationships remains unknown. Here, we combined imaging transcriptomics and in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) to investigate how neurotransmitter receptor organisation relates to local neurochemistry and semantic memory in the human ATL. We found that the ATL exhibited a distinct transcriptomically inferred receptor-subunit profile relative to control cortical regions (occipital cortex and vertex). Individual-specific spatial estimates of receptor-subunit gene expression were systematically associated with local GABA+ and Glx concentrations, revealing preferential coupling between GABAergic receptor genes and GABA+ and between glutamatergic receptor genes and Glx, alongside widespread cross-system associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and Glx. ATL GABA+ and Glx concentrations were positively associated with semantic memory performance, and GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor-subunit expression showed selective relationships with semantic memory accuracy. Crucially, mediation analyses revealed that GABA+ mediated associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and semantic performance, whereas Glx mediated both glutamatergic and widespread GABAergic receptor associations. Together, these findings reveal a coupled molecular-neurochemical architecture of the human ATL, linking neurotransmitter receptor organisation to regional neurochemical state and individual differences in semantic memory. Our findings provide a multiscale account of how cortical molecular organisation is associated with human higher cognitive function.
articles.author: Jung, J., Gim, J.-A., Lambon Ralph, M.

articles.title: Heterogeneous plasticity rules generate diverse structures in recurrent networks
articles.content: How do local changes at individual synapses give rise to structured recurrent connectivity? Experiments have revealed diverse forms of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) across the brain, making it difficult to predict which circuit structures different rules will generate. We developed an analytical framework mapping excitatory Hebbian, anti-Hebbian, and symmetric STDP rules to directed three-neuron motifs. Individual homogeneous rules generate restricted subsets of motifs, and no single rule produces all motifs. Combining different rules generates motifs inaccessible to individual rules and yields the full motif repertoire, and these predictions generalize to larger recurrent networks. The mapping is nevertheless highly non-unique, with distinct rules and parameters producing similar motif distributions, including distributions compatible with experimental connectivity. Thus, circuit structure constrains candidate plasticity rules but does not uniquely identify them. Finally, networks with similar motif distributions can nonetheless differ in their firing rates and pairwise correlations, suggesting that activity may provide an additional constraint on candidate plasticity rules.
articles.author: Cusseddu, C., Festa, D., Miehl, C., Gjorgjieva, J.

articles.title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
articles.content: The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been relatively understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson's Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network, which has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. In a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86 we looked at network connectivity in cognitive and motor sub-circuits. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI). This data was analyzed using the CONN toolbox with an ROI-ROI approach targeting the CB-BG circuit. We replicated the previously mapped cognitive subcircuit and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adult hood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity as it relates to performance on the Stroop task showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. We also explored sex differences and found higher functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. Together, we have replicated motor and cognitive CB-BG subcircuits and further demonstrated that this network has altered connectivity associated with age, sex, progesterone, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential new step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson's Disease.
articles.author: Delaney, C., Herrejon, I., Magalhaes, T. N. C., Jackson, T. B., Hicks, T. H., Bernard, J. A.

articles.title: Ms4a4a loss preferentially remodels microglia with limited, compartment-specific effects across central and peripheral immune compartments in 5xFAD mice
articles.content: Background: Genome-wide association studies have identified the MS4A locus as a major modifier of Alzheimers disease (AD) risk and resilience. MS4A4A is enriched in microglia, and we previously demonstrated that loss of Ms4a4a reduces amyloid plaque pathology and attenuates amyloid-associated tau spreading. However, MS4A4A is also expressed in peripheral myeloid populations, raising the possibility that its effects extend beyond brain-resident microglia. Here, we sought to define how constitutive Ms4a4a loss alters immune populations across central nervous system (CNS), CNS-border, and peripheral compartments in the context of amyloid pathology. Methods: We performed multicompartment immune profiling by flow cytometry in 5xFAD Ms4a4a wild-type and 5xFAD Ms4a4a-deficient mice. Myeloid and lymphoid populations were characterized in the brain, dural meninges, skull bone marrow, tibial bone marrow, and spleen. Results: Ms4a4a loss produced its strongest immune effects in brain microglia. 5xFAD Ms4a4a-deficient mice exhibited increased microglial abundance, increased frequency and expression of CD86, increased MHC class II expression intensity, and enrichment of CXCR4-high microglia, whereas P2RY12 and TREM2 were unchanged. Brain macrophages showed increased MHC class II expression, whereas conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) in the brain showed reduced MHC class II expression, with limited changes in other infiltrating immune populations. Immune composition in the dura and skull bone marrow was largely preserved, although MHC class II expression was increased in skull bone marrow cDCs. Peripheral immune composition in tibial bone marrow and spleen was similarly preserved, with selective increases in M2-like macrophages in tibial bone marrow and splenic CD8 T-cell frequency. Conclusions: These findings identify microglia as the immune population most strongly remodeled by Ms4a4a loss in the setting of amyloid pathology. Constitutive Ms4a4a deficiency does not produce broad systemic immune remodeling but instead preferentially alters microglial state, accompanied by more limited, cell type- and tissue-specific effects across other central and peripheral immune compartments. These findings establish MS4A4A as a context-dependent regulator of immune responses to AD pathology with particularly prominent effects on microglia.
articles.author: Danhash, E., Verbeck, A., Iyer, A., Karch, C. M.

articles.title: Information coding strategies in biological reservoir computing for multiclass time-series classification
articles.content: Physical reservoir computing (RC) using biological neural networks (BNNs) offers a framework for probing how high-dimensional dynamics arising from multicellular systems support complex information processing in the brain. However, how electrical inputs and extracellular readouts should be designed to suit different task demands remains unclear. Here, using primary rat cortical neurons cultured on a high-density microelectrode array, we investigated how input encoding and spike detection methods influence neural representations and the resulting RC performance in BNNs. Comparison of pulse amplitude modulation and latency coding revealed that the latter exhibited superior performance in demanding multiclass conditions, including a 10% improvement in a 10-class spoken digit classification task. Spike sorting further improved classification performance by enhancing class separability, while largely preserving the low-dimensional structure of population activity. These findings highlight the importance of designing information coding strategies according to task difficulty.
articles.author: Nishi, Y., Yamamoto, H., Katori, Y., Sato, S.

articles.title: Focal neuronal loss and cell replacement in a connectome model of fly steering
articles.content: Focal neuronal loss after stroke, traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury can disrupt circuits and result in persistent motor deficits. Which cells and connections must be restored to recover a specific behavior is difficult to establish experimentally. Here we use a connectome-constrained spiking model of the fruit-fly nervous system and decode motor-neuron output to simulate visually guided steering. After loss of 4,000 neurons, path straightness ranged from 0.04 to 0.95 depending on lesion location. At a fixed sensorimotor site, a 2,000-neuron lesion reduced simulated displacement to 6.5% of intact. Across 100 stochastic simulation realizations of the connectome, replacing 100 cells with their original connections increased displacement to 62.5% of intact when motor-control pathways were prioritized, compared with 10.1% after random selection of 100 cells and 48.5% after random selection of 1,000 cells. When connections were instead inferred from cell type, the same 100 intended replacements reached 60.0% of intact with matched identities and 6.7% with non-target identities, indicating that cell identity and type-dependent integration are required for recovery. Our model generates testable predictions for genetic ablation experiments in fruit flies and identifies candidate cellular and circuit requirements for motor repair that can inform cell replacement therapies and future models of mammalian locomotion.
articles.author: Habib, P., Petr, M., Rust, R.

articles.title: A canonical input to the head direction compass carries predominantly eye movement signals
articles.content: The mammalian head direction (HD) system is thought to update its internal compass using angular head velocity (AHV) signals relayed from the brainstem. We tested this canonical interpretation by recording from the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi (NPH), a proposed AHV relay known to be important for accurate HD tracking, while simultaneously measuring eye and head movements in mice. Neurons classified as AHV-tuned instead predominantly encoded eye movements: most showed saccade-related bursts or pauses, and apparent AHV tuning was largely explained by eye rather than head motion. Optotagging showed that even NPH neurons projecting directly to the HD circuit predominantly encoded eye movements. Empirically constrained population models reconstructed eye position and gaze direction, but head-direction readouts failed when eye and head motion were dissociated. These findings overturn the canonical view of NPH as a dedicated AHV relay, revealing eye movements as a major, previously unmeasured component of the signals entering the mammalian HD circuit and thereby changing the computational problem that the HD system must solve to maintain a stable representation of heading.
articles.author: Stott, J. J., Chang, H. H. V., Bao, C., Zhang, K., Cullen, K. E., van der Meer, M. A.

articles.title: High-content imaging of live microglia-containing Alzheimer's disease brain organoids
articles.content: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common progressive neurodegenerative disease for which there is currently no safe and effective treatment. AD is characterized by the pathological aggregation of amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) in the brain resulting in neuronal dysfunction/death and cognitive decline. Modeling these processes in vitro remains challenging due to the lack of an immune-competent 3D in vitro human model of AD amenable to high-throughput analyses. Conventional cerebral organoids (COs) lack microglia and are optically dense which precludes real-time longitudinal analyses. Here, we employ the fluorescent amyloid probe PyrPeg to selectively monitor A{beta} aggregation, and calcein AM and propidium iodide to assess cellular viability within microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We identify age-dependent DS-AD-associated phenotypes within T21 MCOs including A{beta} neuropathology, neurodegeneration, and glial cell dysregulation. Our platform supports real-time, multiplexed tracking of disease progression and provides a scalable platform for longitudinal analyses studying disease mechanisms and targeted approaches to treatment.
articles.author: Quang, D., Summers, R., Dooling, B. R., Esquer, H., Zhou, Q., LaBarbera, D. V., Vergara, M. N., Chial, H. J., Potter, H., Johnson, N. R.

articles.title: Scalp EEG detects motor sequence replay signatures during wakeful rest
articles.content: Brief wakeful rest may support motor-memory processing through replay of recently practiced neural sequences, but human motor replay has been demonstrated mainly with invasive recordings or magnetoencephalography. Here we tested whether ordered motor-sequence replay can be detected from scalp EEG across wakeful rest during motor skill learning. During rest, participants received no cue, regular or accelerated auditory targeted-memory reactivation (TMR), or randomized tones. Neural states re-emerged in the practiced sequence order, revealing forward replay across conditions. Accelerated TMR enhanced total learning; within this condition, stronger forward replay showed the clearest exploratory relationship with micro-offline gains, while forward and reverse replay also covaried with gains across the cohort. The apparent replay timescale shifted systematically with decoder temporal resolution, showing that measured timing reflects both neural dynamics and the observation model. These findings support scalp EEG as a scalable approach for studying ordered motor-sequence reactivation during wakeful rest.
articles.author: Dash, D., Sugata, H.

articles.title: Auditory tracking magnitude, temporal alignment, and anatomical distribution during wakefulness and propofol-based anesthesia in human sEEG
articles.content: General anesthesia attenuates auditory responses, but response magnitude alone does not describe how residual activity aligns with sound over time or varies across the brain. We jointly characterized these aspects of auditory tracking using stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG) in 13 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy during wakefulness and clinically defined unresponsiveness under propofol-based anesthesia. The same rhythmic humming sequences were presented at approximately 1.61 Hz in both sessions. During anesthesia, stimulus-rate power showed widespread reductions and phase alignment with the stimulus rhythm was less consistent, although responses remained detectable at some recording channels. During wakefulness, response strength decreased with cortical surface distance from posteromedial Heschl's gyrus; this distance-response relationship was weaker during anesthesia. In a contrastive learning analysis (CEBRA), low-dimensional embeddings derived from anesthesia recordings yielded lower acoustic-envelope decoding accuracy on held-out data and lower consistency across model fits. Together, these findings characterize how attenuated auditory tracking is expressed jointly in response magnitude, temporal alignment, and anatomical distribution.

Jiang et al. developed a robust postnatal knockout platform for somatosensory genomics and behavioral screening, identifying Creld1 as a cross-modal regulator of somatosensation through its control of sensory neuron excitability via voltage-gated sodium channels.

articles.title: Network geometry shapes the transformation of task representations across the human cortex
articles.content:
Nature Neuroscience, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41593-026-02486-8

The dimensionality of intrinsic brain connectivity systematically shapes how task representations compress and expand across the cortex, and activity flow modeling shows the active role of network geometry in generating the transformation.
